chapter_theme: Fate (ஊழ்): what befalls comes by Nandi's decree and one's own former deeds, so the knowers of truth are unchanged whether they are wounded or anointed. The devotee who has gained the Lord stays with him through thunder, fire, storm and wild beasts, ploughs the field of knowledge, and sees the loss of a body as moving to another house.
structure_note: Fate and the jnani's steadiness (2847 to 2849); the devotee unshaken by disaster (2850, 2851); the death of a body as a change of nest or house (2852).

2847.reading: Whether they are struck or pared away, or anointed with red sandal paste, or a chisel is driven into their heads and they are thrown down, the knowers of truth, who go only by the decree of Nandi the wise, do not decline from their nature.
2847.nuance: விதிவழி அல்லது can be read as 'except by Nandi's decree' (nothing touches them unless he wills it) or as 'going by no way but his decree'. Setting anointing beside the chisel echoes the old ideal of treating the one who wounds and the one who honours alike.

2848.reading: Nothing was made beforehand by the heavens and laid by for one except by the way of the decree one has made oneself; going before the king by the way of the mark on the head, what I did before has become good ground.
2848.nuance: The first two lines make the decree one's own (தான் முன்னம் செய்த விதி), not something heaven stores up. Line 3, கோன் முன்னம் சென்னி குறிவழியே சென்று, is obscure: it may be the mark written on the head (the fate written on the forehead) or the Lord's sign. The poet's former deeds are said to have become நன்னிலம், good ground for the Lord's grace.

2849.reading: The river does not carry the fine sand it has laid down, and no one knows how to divide it up and carry it; my heart, having won Nandi of the ash-smeared body and upright matted hair, cannot part from him.
2849.nuance: The image of the first two lines is not explained and the link to the last two is left to the reader. One possible reading: as the river leaves its sand behind and no one else can carry a share of it, each bears what his own deeds have laid down; another is that what is deposited stays, as the poet's heart stays with Nandi.

2850.reading: What if the sky thunders, what if the great sea surges, what if the red fire of the forest mingles and the body burns, what if the wind strikes fiercely: I, at one with him, will seek the Lord.
2850.nuance: The editor's parallel notes that the opening closely matches a verse of Appar's Thevaram (4.112.8), which uses the same 'what if' (என்) formula for the devotee's fearlessness. தான் ஒன்றி and நான் ஒன்றி both use ஒன்றி (joining): the wind joins its force, the poet joins the Lord.

2851.reading: What if an elephant charges, what if an arrow cuts through, what if a tiger of the forest closes in around: in that other field my Lord has given, I will plough the ploughing of knowledge.
2851.nuance: ஏனைப் பதி (the other place or field) may be the inner field as against the outer world, or the Lord's own realm. The image of ploughing knowledge turns the farmer's labour into spiritual practice.

2852.reading: If the nest perishes, there is one who will make another nest; even if the land perishes, our people do not perish; if the house perishes, it is like entering another house: such is the state of those who know Nandi's nature.
2852.nuance: கூடு (nest, also the body) and வீடு (house, also release) both carry a second sense; the verse's surface sense is that losing a body is like moving house, since the Lord will make another. நமர் (our people) is taken as the Lord's devotees. Whether வீடு here also hints at release is not clear.

links.note: Both ground equanimity in fate: the Kural asks why those who accept good fortune grieve at bad; Tirumular's knowers are unchanged whether anointed with sandal or struck with a chisel, since all comes by Nandi's decree.

The Kural says one enjoys only as the apportioner (வகுத்தான்) apportioned; Tirumular says nothing is laid by from heaven except by the decree one has made oneself, placing the apportioning in one's own former deeds.
Both make fate one's own past deeds: the Naladiyar's old deed finds its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Tirumular's decree is the one 'one made oneself before'.
Both picture the body as a bird's nest or shell the life leaves; the Kural uses it to show how slight the bond of body and life is, Tirumular to say the Lord will build another nest.

The Kural asks whether the life lodging in the body has found no home of its own; Tirumular accepts the body as a passing house and draws comfort from it: losing one is like entering another, for those who know Nandi.

Kural 621 tells one to laugh when trouble comes, since nothing presses back on it as well. 2850 lists thunder, the surging sea, forest fire burning the body and fierce wind (என் ... என்) and answers that, at one with him, he will seek the Lord (நான்ஒன்றி நாதனை நாடுவன்). The same steadiness before calamity appears as worldly resilience in the Kural and as union with the Lord in the Tirumanthiram.

1886 speaks of a seed pot and a fenced field where the ploughing was finished before noon, and of those who cannot lose their fear (அச்சம்கெட்டு) to reap and eat it. 2851 ploughs the ploughing of knowledge (ஞானத்து உழவு) in the field the Lord gave, unmoved by elephant, arrow and tiger. Both make inner practice a ploughing and tie its fruit to fearlessness.

Kural 1031 says that though it is toilsome, ploughing is foremost (உழந்தும் உழவே தலை), since the world follows the plough. 2851 keeps to the ploughing of knowledge (ஞானத்து உழவினை நான் உழுவேனே) though elephant, arrow and tiger threaten. The Kural's ploughing that holds through hardship becomes the jnani's practice that holds through danger.

source_issues: 2850: line 1 reads மாகடல் பொங்கிலன்; the 'what if' pattern of the verse and the editor's parallel (மாகடல் பொங்கிலென்) show it should be பொங்கிலென்.
